approachQuestion.prompt:
Sample shipment

There are n divisible material lots. Lot i has positive mass w[i] and positive total value v[i]; taking any fraction gives that fraction of its value. A container holds at most C mass. The input is already ordered by nonincreasing value per unit mass, with arbitrary ties. Return the maximum total value that can be loaded. Fractions may be arbitrarily fine.

Example 1: lots=[(mass 4,value 12),(mass 6,value 12)], C=5 → 14: take the first lot and one unit of the second.
Example 2: lots=[(3,5)], C=0 → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ w[i],v[i] ≤ 10^6; 0 ≤ C ≤ 10^9. The density ordering is guaranteed, not to be checked. Return an exact rational value; only one selected lot needs to be fractional, and all required products and sums fit 64 bits. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Scan lots in their supplied order. Take each fully while it fits; on the first lot exceeding the remaining capacity, take the fraction that fills the container and stop. Track only capacity and accumulated value.
options.feedback: Exchanging equal mass from a lower-density selected lot to a higher-density omitted lot cannot reduce value. The promised input order therefore allows taking a prefix and at most one fraction. Equal-density ties are interchangeable.

options.text: Find the lot with greatest total value and take as much of it as possible before considering other lots.
options.feedback: Total value ignores mass. For density-ordered lots [(1,10),(10,20)] and C=1 this chooses the second lot and obtains 2 instead of 10.

options.text: Use the supplied order, but skip any lot whose full mass does not fit; take only whole lots.
options.feedback: Divisibility is part of the domain. For lots=[(2,10)] and C=1, skipping gives zero instead of the feasible value 5.

options.text: Copy the input, sort it again by decreasing density using comparison merge sort, then take full lots and one fraction in that order.
options.feedback: This uses the correct density rule, but repeats ordering work that the input contract already guarantees and allocates a needless copy and sorting buffer.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each lot is consumed or fractionally finishes the one-pass capacity fill.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: At most n supplied density-ordered lots are inspected; each full or fractional take performs fixed arithmetic. A capacity exceeding every lot forces all n inspections. Only remaining capacity, value total, and an index are retained, giving O(1) auxiliary space.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
